explanation: Two unrelated triggers: (1) strongest on the ' java'/' javax' token right after 'import' in Java import lists (especially the first java.* import after a block of non-java imports); (2) moderate-to-strong on word-internal subword pieces of Slavic/Central-Eastern European proper names and place names (e.g. 'Kuy[avian]', 'Sp[oko]yny', 'Szpo[j]ankowski', 'Voiv[odes]hip'). Ordinary English words do not fire.

Fires on nouns (and some verbs) about the natural living world: plants, vegetation, crops, species, biomes, ecosystems, animals in ecological context, growth/yield/productivity (e.g. 'vegetation', 'penguins', 'algal blooms', 'reforestation', 'crop yield'). Strongest for ecology/botany terms; food or animals in non-ecological contexts are weak to moderate; unrelated text is near zero.

Fires on tokens inside references to sports competitions, leagues and events, especially the league/competition name words ('MLS Super[Draft]', 'Premier League', 'US Open', 'Copa Libertadores', 'golf course', 'Pro League', 'friendly'). Strongest on the first word of a league/tournament name in sports-reporting context; other sports-narrative words fire moderately; non-sports text does not fire.

Fires mostly in purpose/goal or problem-solving framings: the verb or word after 'how to', 'in order to', 'able to', 'hard to', a sentence-initial 'To X' purpose clause, or the '?'/comma that ends such a how-to question or purpose phrase (e.g. 'how to [market] it', 'To [obtain] a satisfactory', 'To increase revenues[,]'). Some scattered noun-phrase activations in technical abstracts are noise; plain narrative text is weak.

Fires in website/blog/forum blurbs that describe what topics are covered or invite questions: tokens like 'about', 'anything', 'all things', 'topics', 'questions', and the commas/'and'/'|' in lists such as 'News, Editorials, Product Reviews' or 'tips, roundups and news'. Strongest in 'questions about X'/'ask us anything'/'all things X' phrasing; regular prose is weak.

No clear shared feature: fires on assorted tokens, often a noun or determiner that serves as the object/complement right after a verb or preposition ('flippant with his [comments]', 'steer [the] country', 'take care of [the]'), but also on code tokens and math subscripts. Hard to predict.

A mixture: strongly fires on '.S' in 'U.S.C.' legal citations, on URL/file path segments and code/comment tokens ('/', 'httpdocs', 'OpenLayers', '@since', '//', 'core/core'), plus scattered unrelated prose tokens ('peace officer', 'Print', 'component'). No single concept.

Mainly fires on word-internal subword fragments of non-English words (Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Swedish, Turkish) and unusual proper names ('S[mit]a', 'LOUIS[IAN]A', 'Se[leccion]a', 'ch[ius]o'), plus a separate cluster on 'kind' in 'kinda'/'Kind of'. Ordinary English words do not fire.

Fires on boilerplate in source-file headers, especially license/copyright text: 'PROVIDED [BY]', 'WARRANTY [OF]', '[This] file is part of', 'http[://]', comment markers ('//', ' *') and line-ending periods in those headers; also similar formulaic header tokens such as 'No. ' in court captions and closing HTML tags. Ordinary prose is weak.

Mixture of token-level triggers: the subword 'iv' in names/abbreviations ('South-K[iv]u', 'C[iv].', 'Zukowsk[iv]'), the Japanese 'その', subword pieces of names after 'K'/'Q' ('K[evin]', 'K[iki]', 'Q[iz]ilbash'), and other CJK/byte fragments. No unifying concept.

Fires on the head word that completes a multi-word noun phrase or term, i.e. the second element after a modifier ('presidential [candidate]', 'structural [equation]', 'transcription [factor]', 'dendritic [cell]', 'training [camp]', 'Orthopaedic [surgeon]'), plus 'of' in some fixed phrases. The modifier context matters; isolated nouns fire weakly.
